metadata.summary: This guidance updates the World Allergy Organization's 2011 anaphylaxis guidelines, incorporating current knowledge on diagnosis and management. It covers anaphylaxis definition, epidemiology, elicitors, cofactors, severity grading, acute and long-term management, and global availability of epinephrine auto-injectors. The document is intended for healthcare professionals globally, especially in regions without national guidelines.

target_population: patients of any age with anaphylaxis or at risk of anaphylaxis

management.actions: Intravenous epinephrine should be avoided for initial anaphylaxis treatment; if administered, it must be given as an intravenous infusion via pump with cardiac monitoring, and only by personnel experienced in diluting and administering the correct doses.

prevention: Use intramuscular epinephrine as first-line treatment for anaphylaxis.

management.actions: Avoid rapid intravenous administration of first-generation H1-antihistamines; consider using second-generation antihistamines to minimize adverse effects.

prevention: Administer antihistamines cautiously; prefer second-generation agents when available.

management.actions: Substitute with second-generation antihistamines to reduce sedative effects.

prevention: Use second-generation antihistamines in preference to first-generation agents.

toxicities.incidence: Approximately 50% occur within the first 6–12 hours after the initial reaction.
recognition: Return of anaphylaxis symptoms after apparent resolution of the initial episode.

management.actions: Observe patients in a healthcare setting, especially those with severe initial reactions or those requiring multiple doses of epinephrine; extended observation may be warranted.

conditions.name: Anaphylaxis
conditions.description: A serious systemic hypersensitivity reaction that is usually rapid in onset and may cause death. Severe anaphylaxis involves life-threatening compromise of the airway, breathing, or circulation, and can occur without typical skin features or circulatory shock.
conditions.epidemiology: Global incidence is estimated at 50–112 episodes per 100,000 person-years, with a lifetime prevalence of 0.3–5.1%. Pediatric incidence ranges widely, from 1 to 761 per 100,000 person-years. Recurrence rates are 26.5–54% over 1.5–25 years. Mortality remains low: drug-induced anaphylaxis 0.05–0.51 per million people/year, food-induced 0.03–0.32, venom-induced 0.09–0.13.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Acute onset (minutes to several hours) of skin/mucosal involvement (generalized urticaria, pruritus, flushing, angioedema of lips, tongue, uvula) plus at least one of: respiratory compromise (dyspnea, wheeze, stridor, hypoxemia), cardiovascular compromise (hypotension, syncope, collapse), or severe gastrointestinal symptoms (crampy abdominal pain, repetitive vomiting). Alternatively, acute hypotension, bronchospasm, or laryngeal involvement after allergen exposure, even without skin signs. Skin involvement is absent in 10–20% of episodes.

subtypes.name: Food-induced anaphylaxis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Commonly presents with severe gastrointestinal symptoms; triggered by ingestion of allergenic foods such as peanuts, tree nuts, milk, egg, seafood.

subtypes.name: Venom-induced anaphylaxis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Triggered by insect stings (bees, wasps, fire ants); typical systemic reaction with rapid onset.

subtypes.name: Drug-induced anaphylaxis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Occurs after administration of medications (antibiotics, NSAIDs, biologics, chemotherapeutics, contrast media); may be IgE-mediated or non-IgE-mediated.

subtypes.name: Idiopathic anaphylaxis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: No identifiable trigger; accounts for 6.5-35% of cases; requires evaluation for mast cell disorders (mastocytosis, KIT mutation).

subtypes.name: Alpha-gal-induced anaphylaxis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Delayed onset (hours after ingestion of mammalian meat); associated with IgE to galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose.

subtypes.name: Exercise-induced anaphylaxis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Triggered by physical activity, often with cofactors like food ingestion; may involve specific foods (omega-5-gliadin).

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm mast cell activation during an acute episode
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During acute anaphylaxis (within 15 min to 3 h, peak at 1–2 h)
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Elevated levels support anaphylaxis; normal levels do not exclude it. A consensus equation (peak MCT > 1.2 × baseline tryptase + 2 ng/L) may be used.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish individual baseline and detect underlying mast cell disorders
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At least 24 h after resolution of symptoms
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Persistently elevated baseline tryptase suggests mastocytosis or clonal mast cell disease.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify potential triggers, cofactors, and risk factors
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: After acute episode, during specialist assessment

diagnostic_workup.test: Allergen-specific IgE testing and/or skin prick tests

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Rule out clonal mast cell disorder
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In idiopathic anaphylaxis or when baseline tryptase is elevated
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Detection indicates a clonal mast cell disorder (e.g., mastocytosis).

pathology_markers.expected_result: Elevated (>11.4 mg/L) or significant rise over baseline per consensus equation
pathology_markers.clinical_significance: Indicates mast cell degranulation; supports diagnosis of anaphylaxis.

pathology_markers.expected_result: Normal in most individuals; elevated in mastocytosis
pathology_markers.clinical_significance: Elevated baseline increases risk of severe anaphylaxis and suggests need for mast cell workup.

genetic_molecular.technique: PCR from peripheral blood or bone marrow
genetic_molecular.clinical_significance: Identifies clonal mast cell disorder; indicated in idiopathic anaphylaxis or elevated baseline tryptase.

follow_up.schedule: Observe for at least 6–12 hours after reaction, especially if severe or requiring multiple epinephrine doses. Specialist follow-up for trigger identification and education.
long_term_effects: Need for allergen avoidance or immunotherapy
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Patients should carry an epinephrine auto-injector, have a written emergency action plan, wear medical identification, and receive ongoing education on anaphylaxis management.

recommendations.statement: Intramuscular epinephrine (adrenaline) is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis.
All anaphylaxis reactions must be treated with intramuscular adrenaline to reduce the risk of death.
recommendations.context: Emphasized despite most anaphylaxis reactions not being immediately life-threatening.
recommendations.rationale: Fatal outcomes are rare, but unpredictability of progression necessitates treatment.
recommendations.source_heading: DEFINITION AND CLINICAL DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA FOR ANAPHYLAXIS

recommendations.statement: Early suspicion of anaphylaxis, based on symptoms affecting multiple organ systems, should prompt immediate management.

Initial management of anaphylaxis includes removing the trigger if possible, assessing airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, and skin, calling emergency services, injecting intramuscular epinephrine, and positioning the patient.
Intramuscular epinephrine should be injected into the antero-lateral thigh (vastus lateralis muscle).
The recommended epinephrine dose for healthcare professionals is 0.01 mg/kg body weight, up to a maximum total dose of 0.5 mg, administered intramuscularly.
recommendations.context: Simplified dosing table provided: infants under 10 kg: 0.01 mL/kg of 1 mg/mL; children 1–5 years: 0.15 mg; children 6–12 years: 0.3 mg; teenagers and adults: 0.5 mg.

recommendations.statement: Epinephrine dosing may be repeated every 5–15 minutes if symptoms are refractory to initial treatment.
Intravenous epinephrine is not recommended for initial treatment of anaphylaxis due to the risk of fatal arrhythmias from bolus administration.
recommendations.rationale: Intravenous bolus epinephrine can cause fatal arrhythmias.

recommendations.statement: If intravenous epinephrine is used, it should be administered as a continuous infusion via an infusion pump in monitored patients by experienced personnel.
recommendations.context: Low-dose epinephrine infusion protocols exist and have demonstrated safety and efficacy.

recommendations.statement: For upper airway obstruction, consider adding nebulized epinephrine.
High-flow oxygen (preferably 100% via non-rebreather mask) should be administered to all patients with respiratory distress and those receiving repeated doses of epinephrine.
Intravenous access should be established using large-bore cannulae (14 or 16 gauge for adults).
Intravenous crystalloid fluid boluses (20 mL/kg) should be given to patients with cardiovascular instability.
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation with continuous chest compressions should be performed when indicated.
Inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonists (e.g., salbutamol/albuterol) may be used for bronchoconstriction, but are not a substitute for repeated intramuscular epinephrine if symptoms persist.
recommendations.rationale: Bronchodilators do not replace the need for epinephrine.

recommendations.statement: Frequent and regular monitoring of blood pressure, heart rate, perfusion, respiratory status, and mental status is recommended.
H1-antihistamines have a limited role in anaphylaxis treatment but may help relieve cutaneous symptoms; their administration should not delay epinephrine injection.
recommendations.context: Second-generation antihistamines are preferred if available, but first-generation ones are the only parenteral options. Some guidelines now consider antihistamines a third-line treatment.
recommendations.rationale: Antihistamine use can delay more urgent epinephrine administration.

recommendations.statement: Routine use of glucocorticosteroids in acute anaphylaxis is controversial and may not be beneficial; their administration is not essential.
recommendations.context: They are commonly used to prevent protracted symptoms and biphasic reactions, but evidence of benefit is lacking and they may cause harm.
recommendations.rationale: Increasing evidence shows no benefit and potential harm.

recommendations.statement: Parenteral glucagon may be considered in patients with anaphylaxis refractory to epinephrine, particularly those taking beta-blockers.
Patients with anaphylaxis should be observed, especially those with severe reactions or requiring multiple epinephrine doses.
recommendations.context: About half of biphasic reactions occur within 6–12 hours.
recommendations.rationale: Biphasic reactions can occur, necessitating observation.

recommendations.statement: Baseline serum tryptase should be measured at least 24 hours after resolution of anaphylaxis symptoms, even if the acute level was normal.
recommendations.context: Tryptase levels may remain elevated for up to 3 hours; normal levels do not exclude anaphylaxis.
recommendations.rationale: Baseline tryptase helps assess for mast cell disorders and interpret acute increases.

recommendations.statement: A consensus equation (peak MCT > 1.2 × baseline tryptase + 2 ng/L) may be used to diagnose acute mast cell activation, though it cannot detect all anaphylactic reactions.
Individualized anaphylaxis management plans should be part of long-term care for all patients who have experienced anaphylaxis.

At discharge, patients at risk of recurrence should be prescribed self-injectable epinephrine, trained in its use, and provided with a written anaphylaxis emergency action plan and medical identification.

Where epinephrine auto-injectors are unavailable or unaffordable, alternative formulations such as prefilled epinephrine syringes (or 1-mL syringe/needle with ampoule) may be recommended, with adequate training and written instructions.
Patients with anaphylaxis should be referred to an allergy/immunology specialist for confirmation of triggers, prevention advice, and consideration of allergen immunotherapy.
recommendations.context: Idiopathic anaphylaxis is considered after thorough investigation.

recommendations.statement: Vigilant avoidance of culprit allergens is essential to prevent anaphylaxis recurrence.
In medication-induced anaphylaxis, avoidance of the offending drug and use of safe substitutes are mandatory; drug desensitization may be considered if no alternative therapy exists.
Annual follow-up is recommended to review recurrence prevention, epinephrine auto-injector technique, and optimize control of comorbidities such as asthma.
Follow-up with a dietitian and psychologist may be important, as indicated.

therapies_index.name: Epinephrine (adrenaline)
therapies_index.administration: Intramuscular injection into the vastus lateralis of the quadriceps (antero-lateral thigh) at a dose of 0.01 mg/kg (maximum 0.5 mg), repeated every 5-15 minutes if symptoms persist. For self-administration, auto-injectors, prefilled syringes, or ampoule with syringe may be used. In healthcare settings, intravenous infusion (low-dose) via pump may be used for refractory reactions. Nebulized epinephrine may be considered for upper airway obstruction.
key_toxicities: Intravenous bolus can cause potentially fatal arrhythmias
monitoring: Monitor blood pressure, heart rate, perfusion, respiratory status, and mental status

therapies_index.name: Epinephrine auto-injector
approved_indications: Self-treatment of anaphylaxis in community settings
therapies_index.administration: Intramuscular injection into the antero-lateral thigh, holding in place for 3-10 seconds

therapies_index.name: Chlorpheniramine
approved_indications: Relief of cutaneous symptoms in anaphylaxis
therapies_index.administration: Parenteral (intravenous or intramuscular); caution with rapid intravenous administration due to risk of hypotension

therapies_index.name: Diphenhydramine
approved_indications: Relief of cutaneous symptoms in anaphylaxis

therapies_index.name: Clemastine
approved_indications: Relief of cutaneous symptoms in anaphylaxis

therapies_index.name: Hydrocortisone
approved_indications: Used in anaphylaxis to prevent protracted symptoms and biphasic reactions, though evidence of benefit is controversial

therapies_index.name: Methylprednisolone
approved_indications: Used in anaphylaxis to prevent protracted symptoms and biphasic reactions, though evidence of benefit is controversial

therapies_index.name: Glucagon
approved_indications: Refractory anaphylaxis not responding to epinephrine, especially in patients taking beta-blockers

therapies_index.name: Crystalloid intravenous fluid bolus
therapies_index.mechanism: Volume expansion to treat hypotension and shock
therapies_index.administration: Intravenous bolus of 20 mL/kg using crystalloids

therapies_index.name: Allergen immunotherapy
therapies_index.mechanism: Desensitization and induction of tolerance to specific allergens
approved_indications: Prevention of anaphylaxis recurrence, particularly for venom-induced anaphylaxis
therapies_index.administration: Subcutaneous injections of allergen extracts, typically administered in a healthcare setting

therapies_index.name: Drug desensitization
therapies_index.mechanism: Temporary induction of tolerance to a drug through graded administration
approved_indications: Patients with immediate hypersensitivity to a necessary medication when no alternative exists
therapies_index.administration: Graded challenge protocol, typically in an intensive care setting

therapies_index.name: Epinephrine sublingual tablet (RDST)
approved_indications: Potential treatment for anaphylaxis (under development, not yet approved)

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with suspected anaphylaxis, based on acute onset of symptoms involving skin/mucosal tissue plus respiratory compromise, cardiovascular instability, or severe gastrointestinal symptoms; or acute hypotension/bronchospasm/laryngeal involvement after known allergen exposure.
decision_rules: Immediately remove suspected trigger if possible (e.g., discontinue drug infusion).
Assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, and skin.
Call for emergency medical services simultaneously.
Inject epinephrine (adrenaline) intramuscularly into the vastus lateralis (antero-lateral thigh).
Position patient: supine unless respiratory distress (then sitting); if pregnant, left lateral semi-recumbent; if unconscious, recovery position.
Repeat intramuscular epinephrine every 5-15 minutes if symptoms refractory.

If respiratory distress, administer high-flow oxygen (100% non-rebreather mask) and consider nebulized epinephrine for upper airway obstruction or inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonists for bronchoconstriction (not as substitute for epinephrine).
If cardiovascular instability, establish IV access with wide-bore cannula, give IV fluid bolus (20 mL/kg crystalloid), and consider IV epinephrine infusion under expert monitoring if refractory.
Monitor vital signs, cardiac rhythm, and respiratory status frequently; observe for biphasic reaction (at least 6-12 hours, longer for severe reactions).

recommended_regimens.name: Intramuscular epinephrine (adrenaline)
recommended_regimens.summary: First-line treatment for anaphylaxis. Administer 0.01 mg/kg body weight (maximum 0.5 mg per dose) into the antero-lateral thigh, repeated every 5-15 minutes as needed to control symptoms.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Until symptoms resolve; may require multiple doses.

alternative_regimens.name: Intravenous epinephrine (adrenaline) infusion
alternative_regimens.summary: For anaphylaxis refractory to repeated intramuscular epinephrine. Must be administered by experienced personnel with cardiac monitoring, preferably as an infusion via pump. Various low-dose protocols exist (e.g., Brown et al. protocol).
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Refractory anaphylaxis with ongoing cardiovascular or respiratory compromise despite appropriate intramuscular epinephrine.

alternative_regimens.name: Nebulized epinephrine (adrenaline)
alternative_regimens.summary: Consider for upper airway obstruction (e.g., laryngeal edema) as an adjunct to intramuscular epinephrine.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Signs of upper airway obstruction (stridor). Not a substitute for intramuscular epinephrine.

alternative_regimens.name: Inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonists (e.g., salbutamol/albuterol)
alternative_regimens.summary: Adjuvant for bronchoconstriction symptoms after epinephrine administration.

alternative_regimens.name: H1-antihistamines (second-generation oral or first-generation parenteral)
alternative_regimens.summary: May help relieve cutaneous symptoms (e.g., urticaria, pruritus). Limited role; should not delay epinephrine administration. Parenteral first-generation agents (chlorpheniramine, diphenhydramine, clemastine) available; rapid IV administration can cause hypotension. Some guidelines consider them third-line.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Symptomatic relief of skin manifestations only, after epinephrine.

alternative_regimens.name: Glucocorticoids (e.g., intravenous hydrocortisone or methylprednisolone)
alternative_regimens.summary: Historically used to prevent protracted symptoms and biphasic reactions, especially in asthmatic patients. Increasing evidence questions benefit; routine use controversial.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider in moderate-severe anaphylaxis, particularly with asthma, after epinephrine. Not for acute rescue.

alternative_regimens.name: Glucagon
alternative_regimens.summary: Parenteral glucagon may be considered in patients with anaphylaxis not optimally responding to epinephrine, especially those on beta-blockers. Evidence limited.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Refractory anaphylaxis in patients on beta-blockers.

not_recommended.name: Intravenous bolus epinephrine
not_recommended.reason: Risk of fatal arrhythmias; intravenous route should not be used for initial treatment and only as infusion under expert monitoring.

not_recommended.name: Antihistamines as first-line therapy
not_recommended.reason: Do not replace epinephrine; they have a limited role and may delay life-saving epinephrine administration.

not_recommended.name: Glucocorticoids as sole acute treatment
not_recommended.reason: No evidence of benefit in acute anaphylaxis management; routine use is controversial and may be harmful.

response_assessment.method: Frequent monitoring of blood pressure, heart rate, perfusion, respiratory status, and mental status.
response_assessment.interpretation: Reassess for resolution of symptoms or signs of biphasic reaction. Biphasic reactions may occur within 6-12 hours after initial reaction.

response_assessment.method: Observation period of at least 6-12 hours, longer for severe reactions or those requiring multiple epinephrine doses.
response_assessment.interpretation: Ensure no recurrence before discharge; educate patient on risk of biphasic reaction and indications to return.

supportive_care: High flow oxygen (preferably 100% via non-rebreather mask) for respiratory distress or patients receiving repeated epinephrine.
Intravenous access with wide-bore cannula (14 or 16 gauge in adults).
Intravenous crystalloid fluid bolus (20 mL/kg) for cardiovascular instability.
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation with continuous cardiac compressions if indicated.
Positioning: supine with legs elevated (unless respiratory distress); left lateral semi-recumbent if pregnant; recovery position if unconscious.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Pregnant patients: position in left lateral semi-recumbent. Patients on beta-blockers: may require glucagon for refractory symptoms. Self-management: patients at risk should carry epinephrine auto-injector and have a written emergency action plan; instruct on when and how to self-administer epinephrine into the antero-lateral thigh.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients who have experienced anaphylaxis, to prevent recurrences.
decision_rules: Identify trigger(s) through detailed history and confirmatory tests (in vivo and in vitro).
Refer to allergist-immunologist for specialized evaluation.
Provide written personalized anaphylaxis emergency action plan; teach patient/caregiver to recognize symptoms and administer epinephrine promptly.
Prescribe epinephrine auto-injector (or alternative prefilled syringe if auto-injector unavailable); ensure patient/caregiver demonstrates correct technique.
Manage risk factors for fatality: optimize asthma control, address cardiovascular diseases, counsel against risk-taking behaviors, educate on seriousness of anaphylaxis.
Recommend always carrying a mobile phone, especially for exercise-induced anaphylaxis.
Implement measures to avoid triggers: allergen avoidance, allergen immunotherapy (e.g., venom immunotherapy for venom anaphylaxis), drug desensitization when appropriate.
Use medical identification (bracelet/wallet card) indicating allergy.
Document suspected trigger in medical record (electronic/paper).
Provide anaphylaxis education and training to patient, family, and caregivers.
Advocate for public health measures (e.g., improved food labelling).
Schedule follow-up to reassess original cause and management plan.

recommended_regimens.name: Epinephrine auto-injector (or prefilled epinephrine syringe)
recommended_regimens.summary: Carry one or more epinephrine auto-injectors for prompt self-administration in case of recurrence. Inject intramuscularly into antero-lateral thigh, hold for 3-10 seconds, then seek emergency medical help.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: As needed for future reactions; replace before expiration.

recommended_regimens.name: Allergen immunotherapy (e.g., venom immunotherapy)
recommended_regimens.summary: For venom-induced anaphylaxis, allergen immunotherapy is indicated to reduce risk of future systemic reactions.

recommended_regimens.name: Drug desensitization
recommended_regimens.summary: For drug hypersensitivity when the drug is essential and no alternatives exist.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Temporary desensitization; repeated for each treatment course.

response_assessment.method: Review of any subsequent allergic reactions, adherence to avoidance measures, and proper use of epinephrine auto-injector technique.
response_assessment.interpretation: Reassess trigger identification, need for continued immunotherapy, and update action plan.

supportive_care: Anaphylaxis education: train patient and caregivers to recognize early signs and promptly use epinephrine.
Written personalized anaphylaxis emergency action plan.
Public health advocacy for allergen labelling.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: In regions where epinephrine auto-injectors are unavailable or unaffordable, provide alternative such as prefilled epinephrine syringes or vials, with training on proper injection technique. For patients with exercise-induced anaphylaxis, emphasize carrying mobile phone and avoiding exercise alone.

artifacts.title: Current definitions of anaphylaxis in the literature
artifacts.source_heading: DEFINITION AND CLINICAL DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA FOR ANAPHYLAXIS

rows: A serious lifethreatening generalized or systemic hypersensitivity reaction.
A severe lifethreatening generalized or systemic hypersensitivity reaction.
An acute, potentially fatal, multi-organ system, allergic reaction.

Any acute onset illness with typical skin features (urticarial rash or erythema/flushing, and/or angioedema), PLUS involvement of respiratory and/or cardiovascular and/ or persistent severe gastrointestinal symptoms; or Any acute onset of hypotension or bronchospasm or upper airway obstruction where anaphylaxis is considered possible, even if typical skin features are not present.

Anaphylaxis is a serious allergic reaction that involves more than one organ system (for example, skin, respiratory tract, and/or gastrointestinal tract). It can begin very rapidly, and symptoms may be severe or lifethreatening.

Anaphylaxis is a severe, lifethreatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction characterized by being rapid in onset with potentially life-threatening airway, breathing, or circulatory problems and is usually, although not always, associated with skin and mucosal changes.

artifacts.summary: This table compiles definitions of anaphylaxis from various allergy organizations, highlighting the common emphasis on severe, life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reactions.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Understanding the different definitions is crucial for consistent diagnosis and management, as some require multi-organ involvement while others focus on specific clinical features.

artifacts.title: Amended criteria for the diagnosis of anaphylaxis
artifacts.source_heading: DEFINITION AND CLINICAL DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA FOR ANAPHYLAXIS

rows: Acute onset of an illness (minutes to several hours) with simultaneous involvement of the skin, mucosal tissue, or both (eg, generalized hives, pruritus or flushing, swollen lips-tongue-uvula) AND AT LEAST ONE OF THE FOLLOWING: a. Respiratory compromise (eg, dyspnea, wheeze-bronchospasm, stridor, reduced PEF, hypoxemia) b. Reduced BP or associated symptoms of end-organ dysfunction (eg, hypotonia [collapse], syncope, incontinence) c. Severe gastrointestinal symptoms (eg, severe crampy abdominal pain, repetitive vomiting), especially after exposure to non-food allergens

Acute onset of hypotensiona or bronchospasmb or laryngeal involvementc after exposure to a known or highly probable allergend for that patient (minutes to several hours), even in the absence of typical skin involvement.

a. Hypotension defined as a decrease in systolic BP greater than 30% from that person's baseline, OR i. Infants and children under 10 years: systolic BP less than (70 mmHg þ [2 x age in years]) ii. Adults and children over 10 years: systolic BP less than <90 mmHg. b. Excluding lower respiratory symptoms triggered by common inhalant allergens or food allergens perceived to cause “inhalational” reactions in the absence of ingestion. c. Laryngeal symptoms include: stridor, vocal changes, odynophagia. d. An allergen is a substance (usually a protein) capable of triggering an immune response that can result in an allergic reaction. Most allergens act through an IgEmediated pathway, but some non-allergen triggers can act independent of IgE (for example, via direct activation of mast cells).

artifacts.summary: This table presents the revised diagnostic criteria developed by the WAO Anaphylaxis Committee, simplifying the previous NIAID/FAAN criteria into two main conditions based on skin involvement and known allergen exposure.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: These criteria aim to increase sensitivity in identifying anaphylaxis, especially in presentations without skin signs or cardiovascular shock, to ensure timely and appropriate treatment.

artifacts.title: Diagnostic criteria for the diagnosis of anaphylaxis
artifacts.source_heading: DEFINITION AND CLINICAL DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA FOR ANAPHYLAXIS
artifacts.description: The figure illustrates two main diagnostic pathways: 1. If there is acute onset with skin or mucosal involvement (e.g., hives, pruritus, angioedema) PLUS respiratory compromise, reduced blood pressure/end-organ dysfunction, or severe gastrointestinal symptoms, then anaphylaxis is highly likely. 2. If the patient has acute onset of hypotension, bronchospasm, or laryngeal involvement after exposure to a known or probable allergen, even without skin involvement, anaphylaxis should be considered. The criteria emphasize that typical skin features are not always present.
artifacts.summary: This flowchart depicts the amended WAO diagnostic algorithm, simplifying the previous criteria to aid rapid clinical recognition.

artifacts.title: Management of anaphylaxis
artifacts.description: The flowchart outlines the acute management steps: 1. Remove the trigger if possible. 2. Assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, and skin. 3. Call for emergency services. 4. Administer intramuscular epinephrine into the anterolateral thigh. 5. Position the patient supine (or semi-recumbent on left if pregnant, recovery position if unconscious). 6. Upon healthcare arrival, provide high-flow oxygen, establish IV access, give IV fluid bolus for cardiovascular instability, and consider cardiopulmonary resuscitation if needed. 7. For bronchoconstriction, inhaled beta-2 agonists may be given, but epinephrine remains primary. 8. Second-line medications (antihistamines, glucocorticoids) may be considered. 9. Monitor and repeat epinephrine every 5-15 minutes if symptoms persist. 10. Observe for at least 6-12 hours due to risk of biphasic reaction.
artifacts.summary: This algorithm presents a stepwise emergency response for anaphylaxis, emphasizing early intramuscular epinephrine as the cornerstone of treatment.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Following this standardized approach reduces mortality and ensures timely intervention, especially in settings where healthcare professionals may be hesitant to use epinephrine.
